query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, elevated-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere leads to preferential oxidation along grain boundaries (especially of Cr and Ti) that results in brittle oxide precipitates. These oxides reduce grain‐boundary cohesion, causing premature crack initiation and catastrophic failure under thermal/mechanical stress, whereas reducing conditions limit oxide formation and preserve ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix exhibiting typical microstructural features (e.g., minor microsegregation, characteristic grain sizes) from the AM process.
generation.intervention: Switch the atmospheric exposure from a reducing/inert environment to an oxidizing one while holding temperature, time, and stress conditions constant.
generation.conditions: Expose specimens to elevated temperatures (around 800–900°C) for an extended duration (e.g., several hundred hours) under controlled gas atmospheres (one oxidizing with a defined oxygen partial pressure, and one reducing/inert as the baseline). Mechanical stresses (or thermal cycling) may be applied to discern structural integrity changes.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary oxidation state – specifically, the formation of brittle oxide precipitates (e.g., Cr/Ti oxides) along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions at high temperatures, reactive elements (Cr and Ti) form oxides along grain boundaries; the resulting brittle phases compromise grain-boundary cohesion. This microstructural degradation leads to loss of toughness and facilitates crack propagation, culminating in catastrophic failure under mechanical or thermal loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens exposed to the oxidizing atmosphere are predicted to exhibit significant grain-boundary oxidation (observable via microscopy/EDX) with a corresponding reduction in fracture toughness and increased tendency for microcracking and catastrophic failure relative to those in reducing conditions.
generation.baseline: The behavior of specimens exposed to a reducing or inert atmosphere at the same temperature and exposure duration, where minimal grain-boundary oxidation occurs.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for elevated-temperature exposures (approximately 800–900°C) and defined oxygen partial pressures; outside these limits (e.g., lower temperatures or different gas compositions) the governing oxidation mechanism may not dominate the degradation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical oxygen partial pressure and temperature threshold for the transition to catastrophic oxidation-induced embrittlement remain uncertain. Additionally, potential contributions from residual stresses and additive manufacturing-induced microstructural heterogeneities are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens. Expose one group to an oxidizing atmosphere (with a specified oxygen partial pressure) and the other to a reducing or inert atmosphere. Maintain identical exposure conditions (temperature ~800–900°C, duration of several hundred hours, and similar applied stress or thermal cycling) for both groups. Post-exposure, perform detailed microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM with EDX) to evaluate oxide distribution, particularly along grain boundaries, and conduct mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness, tensile testing) to assess degradation.
measurements: Grain-boundary oxide thickness and continuity (via microscopy/EDX)
Crack initiation sites and propagation paths in fracture surfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing atmosphere specimens do not show statistically significant and reproducible increased grain-boundary oxidation and corresponding reduction in mechanical performance (as compared to the reducing atmosphere specimens), then the hypothesis that grain-boundary oxidation is the dominant degradation mechanism will be falsified.
